title: Homily XXVII
subtitle: Matthew VIII. 14, 15.
author: chrysostom
excerpt: Homily XXVII. Matt. VIII. 14. “And when Jesus was come into Peter’s house, He saw his wife’s mother laid and sick of a fever:[R.V., “lying sick of a fever.”]and He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she arose and ministered unto Him.”A.V., “unto them.” [The Oxford edition has “rec. vers.” here. But the word “received” is now applied, in matters of text, only to the editions of Stephens and Elzevir and the readings they contain. The reference is, of course, to the authorized version, and that version in Matt. viii. 15 follows the received text.—R.] But Mark adds also, “immediately,”Mark i. 31. See Luke iv. 39. [Mark’s favorite term, εθς, is rendered “straightway” in the R.V., passim.—R.]meaning to declare the time as well; but this evangelist hath set down only the miracle, without signifying besides the time. And whereas the others say, that she that lay ill did also entreat Him, this too he hath passed over in silence. But this comes not of any dissonance, but the one of brevity, the other of exact narrative. But for what intent did He go into Peter’s house? As it seems to me, to take food. This at least...

footnotes.8: Isa. liii. 4. The Evangelist seems to quote the Hebrew, not the LXX. [The explanation given in the Homily agrees with the LXX., “he bare our sins and suffered pain (ὀ[Greek: δυνται]) on our behalf.” Hebrew has “sorrows” instead of “sicknesses” or “diseases.”—R.]

footnotes.13: i.e., “moderate, as receivers, in what we expect from Him: and averse to all display, when we give in His Name.”
footnotes.19: Matt. xxii. 36; Luke x. 25. [The passage in Luke tells of an entirely different incident. The citation from Matthew is not exact, though “first” occurs in the answer of our Lord.—R.]
footnotes.21: Matt. xix. 16, 17; Luke xviii. 18, 19. [The citation agrees more exactly with Mark x. 18. In Matthew, according to the best mss. authorities, and also the Latin versions and fathers, another form of the answer occurs. Even in Homily LXIII., where the incident is commented upon, Chrysostom does not directly attribute this language, as given above, to Matthew’s Gospel.—R.]
footnotes.27: i. e., of those heretics who “commanded to abstain from meats,” as though possessed with some evil principle: the Manichæan and Marcionite schools. Comp. St. Chrys. on 1 Tim. i. 5.
footnotes.31: Luke ix. 62, [Greek: ἐ][Greek: ν τ βασιλε]. [The citation is peculiar: (1) [Greek: ἐν] is not found in any of our mss. of the New Testament, the received text is [Greek: ε τν βασιλεαν], while the dative alone is better supported. (2) [Greek: τν ορανν] is substituted for [Greek: το θεο;] the former occurring in Matthew only in connection with [Greek: βασιλεα].—R.]
